title: When a child crosses a border
subtitle: Leave to remove, internal relocation and the Hague Convention's summary return mechanism
objectives: Distinguish internal relocation, external relocation (leave to remove) and child abduction, and state which legal framework governs each
Explain how Re F reoriented external relocation around the welfare principle and the welfare checklist, displacing the older Payne guidance as a fixed starting point
Apply the 1980 Hague Convention's habitual-residence trigger and its narrow Article 13 defences to a fact pattern involving a child taken from one Contracting State to another

leadingAuthorities.citation: Re F (A Child) (International Relocation Cases) [2015] EWCA Civ 882
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms that external relocation is decided by applying the welfare checklist directly, not by treating Payne's guidance as a starting presumption

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980
leadingAuthorities.role: The treaty mechanism for the summary return of a wrongfully removed or retained child to their state of habitual residence
Gives the 1980 Hague Convention the force of law in England and Wales
The earlier guidance-led approach to external relocation that Re F moved decisively away from

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often blur three distinct problems into one: a parent wanting to move a child within England, a parent wanting to move a child abroad, and a parent who has already taken a child abroad without consent. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name Re F and the Hague Convention — this lesson checks whether you can tell which one a given fact pattern actually calls for.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans hard on scenario questions: expect to work out whether you're in a relocation dispute or a Hague abduction case before you can answer at all.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the three-way distinction — internal relocation, external relocation, abduction — firmly before moving on; every later part assumes you can sort a fact pattern into the right box.

overview.hook: A mother wants to take her son to live with her parents in Australia. A father discovers, three weeks after the event, that his daughter's mother has taken her to Spain and has no intention of coming back. Both are stories about a child crossing a border. One is decided by asking what is best for this particular child, weighed against a checklist. The other is decided almost without asking that question at all — because the whole point of the mechanism is to get the child back to where the question can be asked properly, by the right court. Confusing the two is the single most common mistake this topic produces.

parts.heading: Three problems that look alike and aren't
parts.voice: structural — sorts the topic before teaching any of it
body: "Can I take my child somewhere else?" is really three different legal questions, and the first job in this area is working out which one you're being asked. Internal relocation is a parent wanting to move within England and Wales — say, from London to Newcastle — against the wishes of the other parent with whom the child has a relationship. External relocation, sometimes still called "leave to remove", is a parent seeking the court's permission to relocate the child permanently outside England and Wales. Both are applications a court decides in advance, on the welfare principle, before any move happens.

Abduction is different in kind, not just degree. It is what the law calls it when a parent removes a child from, or retains a child outside, their habitual residence without the consent of everyone who holds rights of custody, or a court order authorising it. There is no advance welfare hearing, because the whole premise is that one parent didn't wait for one. Where the country of refuge and the child's home state are both parties to the 1980 Hague Convention, a fast, largely fact-light mechanism exists to require the child's swift return — not to decide who should ultimately care for the child, but to put that decision back in the hands of the court best placed to make it.

Internal relocation is the least contentious of the three in law, even though it is often bitterly contested in fact: courts apply the ordinary welfare checklist under s 1 Children Act 1989 (Lesson 9) with no special gloss for the distance involved, though practical questions of contact obviously bear on welfare. This lesson's real work is external relocation and abduction — the two categories where a border crossing changes the legal analysis, not just the geography.

components.definition: Permission a court must give before a child can be permanently relocated outside England and Wales by a parent, where the other parent with parental responsibility does not consent. Decided on the child's welfare as the paramount consideration.

interaction.prompt: A father, without telling the mother, takes their child to live in France, intending never to return. Is this best described as "external relocation" or "abduction"?
options: Abduction — it was done without consent and without a court order
External relocation — any move abroad is relocation regardless of consent
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Relocation is the lawful process of seeking permission in advance; taking a child abroad without consent or a court order authorising it is abduction, whatever the parent's motive.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what's missing here: consent and a court order. "Relocation" describes the application made before a move; a move made without either of those is abduction, however well-intentioned the parent believes themselves to be.

parts.heading: From Payne's guidance to Re F's welfare-first approach
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the doctrinal story in order
body: For over a decade, external relocation applications in England and Wales were shaped by Payne v Payne, a Court of Appeal decision that offered structured guidance: ask whether the applicant's wish to relocate is genuine and reasonable, weigh the likely impact of refusal on the applicant (and, through that, on the child), and only then weigh the effect of the move on the child's relationship with the other parent. In practice, Payne was widely read — and, its critics said, too often applied — as tilting the scales towards the relocating (usually primary-carer) parent, because a refusal was framed as harming that parent's wellbeing, which in turn was said to harm the child.

Payne was never formally overruled, but a series of decisions, culminating in Re F (A Child) (International Relocation Cases), reoriented the law. The Court of Appeal in Re F made clear that Payne's factors are not a free-standing test or a presumption in favour of relocation — they are, at most, a checklist of relevant considerations that a court may find useful, always subordinate to the single paramount question required by s 1 Children Act 1989: what serves this child's welfare, assessed against the full statutory welfare checklist, on these facts.

The practical shift matters for how you write an exam answer. A Payne-era answer might open by asking whether the relocating parent's plan is reasonable. A post-Re F answer opens with the welfare checklist itself — the child's wishes, needs, the likely effect of change, the capability of each parent, and so on — and treats the reasonableness of the applicant's plans as one relevant fact within that broader inquiry, not as the gateway question.

components.factsShort: A mother sought permission to relocate permanently with the child to Germany; the first-instance judge had structured the decision heavily around the Payne guidance.
components.ratioShort: The welfare checklist under s 1 Children Act 1989 is the operative test in every external relocation case; the Payne factors are guidance, not a substitute test or a presumption, and must not be applied mechanically.

expanded.facts: The mother, who was the child's primary carer, applied for permission to relocate permanently with the child to Germany, where she had family and employment prospects. The father opposed the application, arguing it would seriously damage his relationship with the child. The judge at first instance approached the case largely through the structured Payne v Payne framework.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the only test in a relocation case is the paramountcy of the child's welfare, assessed by reference to the welfare checklist. Guidance such as that given in Payne may assist a court in identifying relevant factors, but it must never be treated as imposing a presumption, a starting point, or a substitute for the statutory test itself. Each case turns on its own facts, weighed afresh against the checklist.
expanded.significance: Re F is now the leading modern statement of the law on external relocation. It does not abolish the factors Payne identified as relevant — impact of refusal on the applicant parent remains something a court can weigh — but it strips them of any structural priority, restoring the welfare checklist as the sole operative test.

interaction.prompt: Put these developments in the order they occurred.
items: Payne v Payne sets out structured guidance for external relocation applications
Payne's guidance is criticised for functioning, in practice, as a presumption favouring the relocating parent
A series of Court of Appeal decisions, culminating in Re F, subordinate the Payne factors to the welfare checklist
Modern applications are decided by applying the s 1 Children Act 1989 welfare checklist directly, with Payne's factors as, at most, relevant considerations
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the arc: a structured 2001 test hardens into something close to a presumption in practice, and Re F in 2015 restores the welfare checklist as the sole operative test, demoting Payne to a source of relevant factors only.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — Payne comes first (2001) and sets the structured approach; the criticism and the Re F correction follow it. Re F does not invent a new test so much as put the welfare checklist back at the centre.

parts.heading: Habitual residence: the fact that starts the Hague clock
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the treaty text outward
body: Once you're in Hague Convention territory — a child taken from one Contracting State to another without consent — the entire mechanism turns on a single factual question: where was the child habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention? Get this wrong and you're litigating in the wrong court about the wrong question.

Habitual residence is not defined in the Convention itself. The concept has been developed by case law as a question of fact, not law or presumption: it asks where the child's life was centred, assessed by reference to the degree of integration the child had in a social and family environment in that state — school, activities, relationships, stability — rather than by any fixed period of residence or by parental intention alone. A child can become habitually resident in a new state relatively quickly if the move there is settled and integration begins promptly; equally, a short trip abroad, even a long one, does not by itself shift habitual residence if the child's settled life remains elsewhere.

This matters because the Convention's return mechanism only applies where the removal or retention breached rights of custody actually being exercised under the law of the state of the child's habitual residence immediately before it happened. If a family had already relocated together, in fact and in settled circumstances, before one parent later removed the child from the new state, the new state — not the old one — is where habitual residence, and therefore the Convention's protection, now sits.

components.citation: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980, Article 3
components.text: The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where — (a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention; and (b) at the time of removal or retention those rights were actually exercised, either jointly or alone, or would have been so exercised but for the removal or retention.
elements: Removal or retention across an international border
In breach of rights of custody under the law of the child's habitual residence immediately before the event
Those custody rights were actually being exercised (or would have been but for the removal/retention)

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly shows the child's habitual residence has already shifted to the new state before the removal complained of.
interaction.scenarioText: A family relocated together from England to Canada eighteen months ago, with the children enrolled in Canadian schools and settled into a Canadian home. Six months ago the mother took the children back to England for what she said was a two-week holiday, and has not returned them since. The father, still in Canada, applies for their summary return under the Hague Convention.
tappableSpans: relocated together from England to Canada eighteen months ago
enrolled in Canadian schools and settled into a Canadian home
for what she said was a two-week holiday
interaction.correctSpan: enrolled in Canadian schools and settled into a Canadian home
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the integration evidence. Habitual residence turns on where the child's life was actually centred — school, home, routine — immediately before the retention, not on the length of the original move or the label attached to the later trip.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the evidence of settled, everyday integration into the new state, rather than the dates or the parent's stated reason for the trip — habitual residence is assessed by the child's factual and social integration, not by how long a family has been somewhere or what a parent calls a journey.

parts.heading: The narrow escape hatches: Article 13's defences
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: If a wrongful removal or retention is established and habitual residence is proved, the Convention's default is summary return — the requested court orders the child back to the state of habitual residence so that court can decide the substantive welfare dispute. But Article 13 supplies a short list of defences, and examiners test them precisely because they are drawn deliberately narrow: the Convention would fail at its purpose if defences swallowed the rule.

The two defences students most often need are the grave risk defence and the child's objections defence. Article 13(1)(b) allows a court to refuse return where there is a grave risk that return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm, or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation — a genuinely high threshold, not met merely because return would be disruptive, upsetting, or a worse outcome than the child staying where they are. Article 13 also allows a court to take account of the child's own objections to return where the child has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of their views — again a discretion, not an automatic bar, and the objection must be to returning to the state of habitual residence, not simply a preference to remain with the abducting parent.

Both defences are gateways to a discretion, not automatic outcomes: even where a defence is made out, the court retains a discretion whether to order return anyway. Courts guard this discretion carefully, precisely because the whole architecture of the Convention depends on states trusting each other not to let their own courts re-litigate the merits under the guise of a narrow defence.

components.label: Article 13's narrow defences
points: Grave risk (Art 13(1)(b)) — return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm, or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation; a high threshold, not met by mere disruption
Child's objections (Art 13) — the child objects to return and has attained an age and maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of their views
Both are gateways to a discretion to refuse return, not automatic bars — the court can still order return even where a defence is technically made out
Neither defence permits the requested court to re-decide who should ultimately care for the child — that question belongs to the state of habitual residence

interaction.prompt: Under Article 13(1)(b), which of these is closest to the correct threshold for the grave risk defence?
options: A grave risk that return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm, or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation
Any risk that the child will be unhappy or unsettled by the return
A risk that the abducting parent will find the return emotionally difficult
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Article 13(1)(b)'s language is deliberately demanding — 'grave risk' and 'intolerable situation' — precisely so that ordinary disruption or a parent's own distress cannot defeat the Convention's return mechanism.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The Convention's own wording sets a high bar on purpose: 'grave risk' of harm or an 'intolerable situation', not mere unhappiness, disruption, or the emotional cost to the abducting parent. A lower threshold would let the exception swallow the rule.

parts.heading: Why a Hague hearing is not a custody hearing
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Here's the question that trips students up most: if a court hearing a Hague application thinks the abducting parent is actually the better carer, can it refuse return on that basis? The answer is no, and understanding why is the key to this whole area.

The 1980 Hague Convention deliberately does not ask which parent should have custody, or where the child's welfare would ultimately be best served in the broadest sense. It asks a narrower, faster question: was this child wrongfully removed or retained from their state of habitual residence, and if so, should they be summarily returned there so that the courts of that state — usually better placed, with fuller evidence, established jurisdiction and often the other parent's own legal system — can decide the real welfare question properly? Summary return is a jurisdictional remedy, not a merits decision.

This is precisely why the Article 13 defences are read narrowly and why the discretion to refuse return, even once a defence is technically established, is used sparingly. If courts routinely allowed a Hague hearing to become a full welfare inquiry, the Convention's central promise — that a state won't become a haven for one parent's unilateral decision simply because they got there first and found a sympathetic judge — would collapse. Compare this with Re F: in an external relocation application, the welfare checklist is exactly the inquiry the court is meant to conduct in full. In a Hague case, that same full inquiry is the very thing the Convention is designed to send back to the right court, not to conduct itself.

components.title: Relocation dispute or Hague abduction case?
components.description: A flowchart for sorting a border-crossing fact pattern into the right legal framework.

nodes.label: Has the child already been taken across an international border without consent or a court order?
No → this is a prospective application: internal relocation (s 1 CA 1989) or external relocation / leave to remove (welfare checklist, Re F)
Yes → is the country of refuge a Hague Convention Contracting State along with the child's home state?
Yes → Hague Convention summary return mechanism: prove wrongful removal/retention from habitual residence; consider narrow Art 13 defences
No → non-Hague route: inherent jurisdiction, wardship, or the receiving state's own domestic welfare proceedings (outside this lesson's scope)

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the child has already been taken across a border without consent or a court order. If not, this is a prospective relocation application, decided on the welfare checklist (internal relocation under s 1 Children Act 1989, or external relocation applying Re F). If the child has already been taken, ask whether both the country of refuge and the child's home state are Hague Convention parties. If so, the Hague summary return mechanism applies: prove wrongful removal or retention from habitual residence, then consider the narrow Article 13 defences. If not, a non-Hague route applies instead.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is the court's task to conduct a full welfare inquiry, rather than to decide a narrow question about return?
interaction.scenarioA: A mother has already taken the children to Italy without the father's consent; he applies under the Hague Convention for their summary return to England, their home before the move.
interaction.scenarioB: A mother applies to the English court in advance for permission to relocate permanently with the children to Italy, which the father opposes.
interaction.explanation: B is an external relocation application: the court applies the s 1 welfare checklist directly, per Re F, and decides the full merits of whether the move serves the children's welfare. A is a Hague case: the court's task is the narrower question of wrongful removal and habitual residence, with the full welfare merits reserved for the courts of the child's home state.

testPool.prompt: Name the case that reoriented external relocation law around the s 1 Children Act 1989 welfare checklist, displacing Payne v Payne's guidance as a starting point.
testPool.modelAnswer: Re F (A Child) (International Relocation Cases) [2015] EWCA Civ 882, which held that the welfare checklist is the operative test, with Payne's factors as, at most, relevant considerations.

testPool.prompt: Name the single factual question that triggers the 1980 Hague Convention's return mechanism.
acceptableAnswers: where the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention
testPool.modelAnswer: Where the child was habitually resident immediately before the wrongful removal or retention — habitual residence is the jurisdictional trigger for the whole mechanism.

testPool.prompt: Does the 1980 Hague Convention give the requested court the power to decide, as a merits question, which parent should have custody of the child?
options: No — its return mechanism is a jurisdictional remedy, not a custody decision
Yes — Hague proceedings are a full custody hearing

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the narrow Article 13 defences to a Hague return application?
options: Grave risk of harm or an intolerable situation on return
The child's objections, where they have attained sufficient age and maturity
The abducting parent believed, in good faith, that relocation was in the child's best interests
testPool.trapExplanation: A parent's sincere belief that the move was best for the child is not a recognised Article 13 defence at all — however genuine the motive, it does not excuse a wrongful removal or retention, and confusing motive with a defence is one of the most common exam errors in this area.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps a court works through when deciding a Hague Convention return application.
items: Determine the child's habitual residence immediately before the removal or retention
Decide whether the removal or retention breached rights of custody actually being exercised there
If wrongful removal/retention is established, consider whether a narrow Article 13 defence is made out
Exercise the residual discretion whether to order return, even if a defence is technically established

testPool.prompt: Under Article 3 of the 1980 Hague Convention, a removal or retention is 'wrongful' only where custody rights under the law of the child's habitual residence were being exercised, or would have been but for the removal. What is the practical effect of this second limb?
options: A parent who was not, in fact, exercising their custody rights before the removal cannot rely on the Convention as if they had been, absent an explanation for why they weren't
It means any parent with parental responsibility can always invoke the Convention regardless of their prior involvement
It has no practical effect and is rarely litigated

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Re F, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The judge at first instance structured his decision heavily around the guidance given in Payne v Payne. That approach was mistaken. The only test to be applied in a case of this kind is the paramountcy of the child's welfare, assessed by reference to the statutory welfare checklist; guidance such as that in Payne may assist in identifying relevant factors, but must never be elevated into a presumption or a substitute for the statutory test itself.
testPool.ratioSentence: The only test to be applied in a case of this kind is the paramountcy of the child's welfare, assessed by reference to the statutory welfare checklist; guidance such as that in Payne may assist in identifying relevant factors, but must never be elevated into a presumption or a substitute for the statutory test itself.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most strongly support a grave risk defence under Article 13(1)(b), as opposed to ordinary disruption from the move.
testPool.scenarioText: A father applies for the summary return of his children to their home state. The mother, who removed them, says returning would mean the children changing school again and missing their friends, and that the father has a documented history of serious violence towards her in the family home, witnessed by the children on more than one occasion.
tappableSpans: a documented history of serious violence towards her
witnessed by the children on more than one occasion
testPool.correctSpan: a documented history of serious violence towards her
testPool.explanation: Changing school and missing friends are the ordinary, foreseeable costs of any return and do not meet Article 13(1)(b)'s high threshold. Documented serious violence, particularly witnessed by the children, is the kind of evidence capable of establishing a grave risk of physical or psychological harm.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is governed by the s 1 Children Act 1989 welfare checklist directly, rather than by the Hague Convention's wrongful removal framework?
testPool.scenarioA: A father wants to move with the children from Bristol to Leeds for a new job; the mother objects and he applies to the court for permission.
testPool.scenarioB: A father has already taken the children from their home in Bristol to live permanently in Portugal without the mother's knowledge or consent.
testPool.explanation: A is internal relocation within England and Wales, decided under s 1 Children Act 1989's welfare checklist with no Hague dimension at all. B is a wrongful removal engaging the Hague Convention's return mechanism instead, since it has already happened and crosses an international border without consent.

testPool.prompt: A 14-year-old, habitually resident in Ireland, is retained in England by one parent after a holiday. She tells the court clearly and coherently that she does not want to go back to Ireland, where she has few friends and struggled at school, and that she would rather stay with the parent who kept her in England. What is the most accurate statement of her objection's legal significance?
options: Given her age, the court may take account of her objection as a discretionary factor under Article 13, but it is not an automatic bar to return
Her objection automatically prevents return regardless of any other factor
A child's views are irrelevant to a Hague application
testPool.explanation: At 14, she plausibly has the age and maturity for her views to be taken into account under Article 13 — but the defence is a gateway to a discretion, not an automatic bar. The court can still order return even having considered her objection.

testPool.prompt: A family lived together in the Netherlands for three years, with the children enrolled in Dutch schools. Following the parents' separation, the mother brought the children to England for a fortnight's holiday, agreed in advance with the father, but did not return them at the end of it and has since enrolled them in an English school. The father applies to the English court for their summary return under the Hague Convention. Analyse the application.
factsToOrder: The family lived together in the Netherlands for three years with settled schooling
The mother's trip to England was agreed as a fortnight's holiday, not a relocation
The children were not returned at the end of the agreed period
The mother has since enrolled the children in an English school

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the children's retention in England beyond the agreed holiday period is a wrongful retention under the Hague Convention, triggering the summary return mechanism.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Article 3, a retention is wrongful where it breaches custody rights actually being exercised under the law of the state of the child's habitual residence immediately before the retention. Habitual residence turns on the child's factual and social integration, not on the length or label of a later trip abroad.
modelAnswer.application: The children's settled life — three years, established Dutch schooling — was centred in the Netherlands immediately before the trip to England, so the Netherlands remains their habitual residence at the relevant time; a fortnight's agreed holiday does not shift it. The mother's failure to return them at the end of the agreed period, followed by enrolling them in an English school, is evidence of an intention not to return, not evidence that habitual residence had already moved — habitual residence is assessed as at the moment of the wrongful act, not retrospectively justified by what the retaining parent does afterwards.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The retention is wrongful: the children were habitually resident in the Netherlands immediately before it, and the father's custody rights were being exercised there. The English court should proceed towards ordering summary return, subject to any Article 13 defence the mother raises and can substantiate.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a parent's genuine, reasonable wish to relocate automatically entitles them to leave to remove a child under Re F?
sliderLabels: Definitely not automatic under Re F
testPool.correctPosition: Definitely not automatic under Re F
testPool.explanation: Not automatic. Re F treats the reasonableness of a parent's plans as, at most, one relevant factor within the s 1 welfare checklist — never a determinative or presumptive one on its own.

testPool.prompt: Which Act gives the 1980 Hague Convention the force of domestic law in England and Wales?
options: Child Abduction and Custody Act 1985
Children Act 1989
Family Law Act 1996
testPool.explanation: The Child Abduction and Custody Act 1985 incorporates the 1980 Hague Convention into domestic law, giving its return mechanism direct legal effect in England and Wales.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures why the Article 13 defences are interpreted narrowly?
options: Because the Convention's central purpose — deterring unilateral removal by ensuring swift return — would be undermined if defences allowed the requested court to re-litigate the welfare merits
Because Article 13 was drafted with a typographical error that courts have chosen to ignore
Because most abducting parents are found to be lying about their reasons for leaving
testPool.trapExplanation: The narrow reading isn't about doubting parents' honesty or a drafting quirk — it follows directly from the Convention's structural purpose. A generously read exception would let the exception swallow the rule and defeat the whole point of a fast, trust-based return mechanism between states.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the wrong framework — reasoning about a Hague abduction case as though it were a welfare-checklist relocation dispute, or vice versa. Sort the fact pattern first: has the child already been taken, and is this a Hague-Contracting-State problem, before reaching for either test.
